claims.text: The starting alloy has the composition W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The starting W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is nanocrystalline.
The starting alloy is prepared by powder metallurgy or sintering.
Slight compositional inhomogeneity in the starting alloy predisposes it to irradiation-induced Cr–V clustering.
A suitably chosen post-sinter anneal will promote solute diffusion and eliminate compositional gradients and microsegregation inherited from sintering.
Improved chemical homogeneity will reduce the thermodynamic driving force for Cr–V precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Post-sinter annealing will enhance vacancy–interstitial recombination.
High vacancy–interstitial recombination can limit irradiation-induced loop and cavity accumulation in W–Ta–Cr–V refractory alloys.
Irradiation-defect clusters can act as nucleation sites for Cr–V precipitation in this alloy.
The post-sinter anneal will suppress irradiation-induced Cr–V precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
After approximately 8 dpa, the annealed alloy will have a significantly lower Cr–V precipitate density, potentially complete absence of such precipitates, relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy forms Cr- and V-rich precipitates under irradiation.
The precipitates in the untreated alloy are nanoscale and form under conditions similar to approximately 8 dpa.
The untreated alloy exhibits negligible or low irradiation hardening near 8 dpa.
The annealed alloy will retain the negligible irradiation hardening of the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-defect-cluster growth than the untreated alloy.
Post-sinter annealing will improve bulk fabricability by reducing residual stresses and producing a more consistent microstructure.
Energetic-particle irradiation at roughly 773–1050 K and approximately 8 dpa represents an applicable fusion-relevant test range for the hypothesis.
Keeping the annealing temperature below the solvus and grain-growth thresholds will preserve nanocrystallinity.
